chapter_title: Geotechnical Issues in Pavement Design and Performance

sections.title: Basic Concepts - Layered System and Moisture Sensitivity
sections.summary: A pavement is a layered system that must provide structural capacity, ride quality, and skid resistance with adequate durability. Traffic-induced stresses are highest in the upper layers and attenuate with depth (Figure 3-1), so higher-quality, more expensive materials are placed near the surface and lower-quality, cheaper materials deeper (Figure 3-2). The unbound soil layers carry a substantial part of the structural capacity - often more than 50% for flexible pavements. Moisture is the dominant environmental factor: water entering by surface infiltration, edge inflow, or capillary rise from the water table reduces the strength and stiffness of unbound materials, promotes fines migration, and can cause swelling (frost heave, expansion) and subsequent consolidation.
sections.body: Pavements are layered systems designed to (1) provide a strong structure to support traffic loads (structural capacity), (2) provide a smooth wearing surface (ride quality), and (3) provide a skid-resistant surface (safety), with sufficient durability so the system does not deteriorate prematurely from environmental influences (water, oxidation, temperature). The unbound soil layers provide a substantial part of the overall structural capacity, especially for flexible pavements (often more than 50%). Because traffic-induced stresses are highest in the upper layers and diminish with depth (Figure 3-1), higher-quality and generally more expensive materials are used in the more highly stressed upper layers (surface, base) and lower-quality, less expensive materials in the deeper layers (subbase, subgrade) (Figure 3-2). This optimization minimizes cost and allows use of locally available materials but requires greater attention to the lower-quality layers (the subgrade) to reduce life-cycle cost, since good long-term performance of the lower layers lets the upper layers be rehabilitated rather than fully reconstructed. As with all geotechnical structures, pavements are strongly influenced by moisture: water migrates in through surface infiltration (cracks), edge inflows (inadequate ditches/shoulders), and the underlying groundwater table (capillary rise in fine-grained soils), and in cold climates undergoes seasonal freeze/thaw. Moisture nearly always degrades performance - it reduces strength and stiffness of unbound materials, promotes contamination of coarse granular material by fines migration, and can cause swelling (frost heave, soil expansion) and consolidation, as well as spatial variability manifested as local distress (potholes) or roughness. Geotechnical pavement design therefore focuses on moisture-insensitive free-draining base/subbase materials, stabilization of moisture-sensitive subgrades, and adequate drainage of infiltrated water.
key_points: Pavement objectives: structural capacity, ride quality, skid resistance, durability
Unbound soil layers carry a large share of structural capacity (>50% for flexible pavements)
Traffic stresses highest at surface, attenuate with depth (Figure 3-1) -> better materials near top, cheaper materials deeper (Figure 3-2)
Moisture is the dominant environmental factor and nearly always degrades performance
Water enters by surface infiltration, edge inflow, and capillary rise from the water table
Moisture reduces strength/stiffness, promotes fines migration, and causes swelling (frost heave/expansion) and consolidation
Design focus: moisture-insensitive free-draining base/subbase, subgrade stabilization, drainage

sections.title: General Issues - New vs. Rehabilitation vs. Reconstruction; Natural Subgrade vs. Cut vs. Fill; Environmental Effects
sections.summary: Whether a project is new construction, rehabilitation, or reconstruction sets the tone for the geotechnical work. New construction needs comprehensive conventional site characterization (maps, borings, lab tests, geophysics) covering both cut and fill. Rehabilitation and reconstruction can draw on original design/as-built records plus new borings, DCP, and FWD nondestructive testing. Cut sections raise drainage and cut-slope-stability concerns; fill sections raise embankment slope stability and settlement (compression of fill plus consolidation of soft foundation soils), though a compacted fill subgrade is often higher quality than the natural soil. Environmental effects (moisture and temperature) strongly influence layer moduli: asphalt modulus varies with temperature, freezing can raise unbound modulus 20-120x, thawed/trapped water sharply weakens geomaterials, and unbound stiffness falls as moisture content rises.
sections.body: The first issue in any pavement design is whether the project is new construction (new alignment), rehabilitation (repair/upgrade of an in-service pavement, e.g. AC overlays, partial/full-depth recycling), or reconstruction (complete removal down to and including the upper foundation soil, then replacement). New construction is the traditional design focus but agencies have shifted toward rehabilitation and reconstruction. New construction typically requires substantial conventional site characterization (geological/soil maps, boring programs, laboratory testing, geophysics; Chapter 4) over both cut and fill conditions, often with limited access. Rehabilitation can use original design and as-built records for background, but properties (e.g. subbase stiffness) may have changed (fines contamination), so new tests are taken from borings through the existing pavement or via in-situ tests like the Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP); falling weight deflectometer (FWD) nondestructive evaluation is very common, and forensic distress evaluation helps identify deficiencies. Since the unbound layers are not exposed in rehabilitation, their deficiencies must be compensated by added surface-layer capacity. Reconstruction also uses original records for the subsurface profile (still relevant) but not the original material characterization (those materials are removed); foundation properties come from records, borehole sampling/testing, and FWD, similar to rehabilitation. NATURAL SUBGRADE vs. CUT vs. FILL: the natural-subgrade case is the textbook one, with profile and subgrade properties taken directly from exploration. Cuts add drainage concerns (surrounding ground slopes toward the pavement, water table nearer the section), possible stabilization of moisture-sensitive soils, and cut-slope stability (usually treated separately); transition zones (e.g. cut to at-grade) need attention for nonuniform support and water flow. Fills are built of well-compacted material, often producing a subgrade better than the natural soil; the main concerns are embankment slope stability and settlement (compression of the fill plus consolidation of soft foundation soils beneath), usually evaluated as part of the roadway embankment design. ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS: moisture and temperature drive layer and subgrade properties. Asphalt-bound modulus varies strongly with temperature (about 2-3 million psi (14,000-20,000 MPa) in cold winters down to about 100,000 psi (700 MPa) in hot summers); cementitious flexural strength/modulus are less temperature-sensitive, but temperature and moisture gradients induce stresses in rigid slabs. At freezing, the resilient modulus of unbound materials can rise 20-120x, but ice-lens formation and subsequent spring thaw (water trapped above a still-frozen zone) create zones of greatly reduced strength. Unbound stiffness decreases as moisture content increases (a fivefold modulus change is possible between wet and dry), via both stress-state (suction/pore pressure) and structural (loss of inter-particle cementation) effects.
key_points: Project type (new / rehabilitation / reconstruction) governs the characterization approach
New construction: comprehensive conventional exploration over cut and fill (Chapter 4)
Rehabilitation/reconstruction: original records + borings + DCP + FWD nondestructive testing
Rehab deficiencies in buried unbound layers must be offset by added surface capacity
Cut sections: drainage and cut-slope stability concerns; watch transition zones
Fill sections: embankment slope stability and settlement (fill compression + foundation consolidation); compacted fill often beats natural subgrade
Asphalt modulus varies strongly with temperature; freezing raises unbound Mr 20-120x; spring thaw sharply weakens geomaterials
Unbound stiffness falls as moisture rises (up to ~5x) via suction/pore-pressure and loss of cementation
sections.applicability: Scoping the geotechnical exploration and design approach by project type and cut/fill condition, and accounting for moisture/temperature effects on layer properties

sections.title: Specific Issues - Material Types, Drainage, Special Conditions, and Soil Improvement
sections.summary: The major pavement material types are catalogued in Table 3-1 (asphalt, PCC, cementitiously stabilized, non-stabilized granular base/subbase, subgrade soils by USCS/AASHTO class, and bedrock). Properties of interest fall into physical, stiffness/strength, thermo-hydraulic, and performance-related categories; stiffness (resilient modulus) is the single most important geotechnical property. Drainage is critical - the three approaches are to prevent water entering, use moisture-insensitive materials/features, and quickly remove water that does enter (Figure 3-3). Special problem conditions are frost (heave plus spring thaw-weakening), swelling/expansive soils (over $1 billion/yr damage), and collapsible soils (e.g. loess). Soil improvement spans blending and mechanical stabilization (compaction), admixture stabilization (lime, cement, bituminous, pozzolans; Table 3-2), geosynthetics, and - for very soft soils - special ground-improvement (wick drains, surcharge, lightweight fill, piled embankments).
sections.body: MATERIAL TYPES AND PROPERTIES: the major material types in pavement systems are listed in Table 3-1 (NCHRP 1-37A): asphalt materials, PCC materials (intact and fractured slabs), cementitiously stabilized materials (cement-stabilized, soil cement, lime-cement-flyash, lime-flyash, lime stabilized/modified soils), non-stabilized granular base/subbase (including recycled RAP), subgrade soils (grouped by USCS/AASHTO class from gravelly A-1/GW to high-plasticity clays A-7/CH), and bedrock (solid/massive vs. highly fractured/weathered). The geotechnical focus is non-stabilized granular base/subbase, non-stabilized and stabilized subgrade soils, and bedrock. Properties of interest are organized as physical (classification, density, water content), stiffness/strength (resilient modulus, modulus of subgrade reaction k, CBR), thermo-hydraulic (drainage coefficients, permeability, thermal expansion), and performance-related (repeated-load permanent deformation). Stiffness, quantified by the resilient modulus, is the most important geotechnical property and is used explicitly in most design procedures (1993 AASHTO); mechanistic-empirical procedures (NCHRP 1-37A) need more property information, especially thermo-hydraulic and performance behavior. Shallow bedrock (less than 3 m (10 ft) deep) must be considered in construction, design, and performance - notably in FWD backcalculation. DRAINAGE: excess moisture combined with heavy traffic and moisture-susceptible materials reduces service life, and freezing worsens it. Moisture comes from a high groundwater table (upward seepage), lateral edge/shoulder flow, and - most significant - infiltration through surface joints, cracks, and defects (Figure 3-3). The three main control approaches are: (1) prevent moisture from entering (adequate cross/longitudinal slopes for runoff, seal cracks/joints); (2) use moisture-insensitive materials and design features (granular materials with few fines, cement/lean-concrete/asphalt-stabilized bases; dowel bars, widened slabs, subbases for rigid pavements; full-width paving and stabilized base for flexible pavements); and (3) quickly remove water that enters (underdrains and ditches to lower the water table; permeable bases and edgedrains to remove infiltration). Drainage design is detailed in Chapter 7. SPECIAL CONDITIONS: frost heave (requires a frost-susceptible soil, freezing temperatures, and available water; the major damage is spring-thaw weakening, with winter heave reducing serviceability); swelling/expansive soils (localized volume change as roadbed soils absorb moisture, estimated to cause well over $1 billion/year in pavement damage); and collapsible soils (metastable structures - typically silty loess - that lose large volume on saturation; native collapsible subgrades are pre-wetted and heavily rolled, and embankments over them may need special remediation). Identifying problem soils is a primary objective; mitigation is detailed in Chapter 7. SOIL IMPROVEMENT: natural site soils are often unsuitable (poor gradation, inadequate strength/stiffness, instability against swelling). Deficiencies can be addressed by blending soils and mechanical stabilization (compaction), or by admixture stabilization (bituminous binders, lime, Portland cement, or pozzolans) which improves strength/stiffness and also workability, swell reduction, and construction platform. Geosynthetics serve as reinforcement and as filter/drainage layers. In extreme soft-soil conditions, special ground-improvement (wick drains, piled embankments, surcharge, lightweight fill such as geofoam) may be required, usually evaluated by the geotechnical unit. Common stabilization methods, suitable soils, and intended effects are summarized in Table 3-2 (Rollings and Rollings, 1996): blending improves gradation/plasticity, lime suits plastic soils (drying, strength gain, plasticity reduction, long-term pozzolanic cementing), cement suits plastic and coarse soils (cementing of grains), and bituminous suits coarse/some-fines materials (strengthen/bind/waterproof).

Properties grouped: physical, stiffness/strength, thermo-hydraulic, performance-related; resilient modulus is the most important
Shallow bedrock (<3 m / 10 ft) matters for construction, design, performance, and FWD backcalculation
Three drainage approaches: prevent entry, use moisture-insensitive materials/features, quickly remove water (Figure 3-3)
Special soils: frost (heave + spring thaw-weakening), expansive (>$1 billion/yr damage), collapsible (loess)
Soil improvement: blending + mechanical stabilization, admixtures (lime/cement/bituminous/pozzolan), geosynthetics
Very soft soils may need special ground improvement (wick drains, surcharge, lightweight fill, piled embankments)

sections.title: Sensitivity of Pavement Design to Geotechnical Factors
sections.summary: Geotechnical inputs are intimately tied to pavement design. Subgrade stiffness/strength is a direct design input: Figure 3-4 shows that as subgrade CBR rises from 2 to 50, the unbound granular base's contribution to structural capacity in a 1993 AASHTO flexible design falls from about 50% to essentially zero; Figure 3-5 shows the parallel effect of base quality. Subgrade support drives cost - e.g. dropping subgrade CBR from 8 to 4 raises a flexible pavement's cost by more than 20% (Figure 3-6). Some important geotechnical factors (such as a slope failure beneath a side-hill cut, Figure 3-7) cannot be captured explicitly in conventional pavement design even though they can be far more devastating than inadequate subgrade stiffness.
sections.body: Although the surface course is the single most significant layer for pavement performance, the geotechnical layers are intimately intertwined with the design. Subgrade stiffness/strength is a direct input to most design procedures, so its impact can be evaluated quantitatively. Figure 3-4 shows the influence of subgrade California Bearing Ratio (CBR) on the required thickness and structural-capacity contribution of the unbound granular base in a 1993-AASHTO flexible design: the base's contribution to overall structural capacity falls from about 50% at a low CBR of 2 to essentially zero at a high CBR of 50 (assumptions: W18 = 10M ESALs, 85% reliability, So = 0.4, delta-PSI = 1.7, a1 = 0.44, a2 = 0.14, m2 = 1). Figure 3-5 shows the analogous influence of base-layer quality (base CBR) on required AC thickness. A good overall indicator of sensitivity is the impact of subgrade support on cost (Figure 3-6): at 10 million ESALs and subgrade CBR = 8, the cost is about $12,800 per 1000 sq yd (850 m2) of surface; at CBR = 4 the same section costs about $15,600, or more than 20% more (unit costs: asphalt $1.25/in, untreated base $0.30/in, granular borrow $0.20/in; thicknesses at 90% reliability; minimum granular thickness 6 in). It is important to recognize that while many geotechnical factors can be incorporated explicitly, others cannot - for example, the potential for a slope failure beneath a pavement on a side-hill cut is not part of conventional pavement design even though such a failure (Figure 3-7) can be far more devastating to the pavement than inadequate subgrade stiffness.
key_points: Subgrade stiffness/strength is a direct input to most pavement design procedures
Figure 3-4: base contribution to structural capacity falls ~50% (CBR=2) to ~0% (CBR=50) in 1993 AASHTO flexible design
Figure 3-5: base CBR quality controls required AC thickness
Figure 3-6: lowering subgrade CBR from 8 to 4 raises flexible pavement cost by >20%
Some critical geotechnical factors (e.g., slope failure under a side-hill cut, Figure 3-7) are not captured in conventional pavement design but can be far more damaging

sections.title: Pavement Design Methodologies - Empirical, Mechanistic, and Mechanistic-Empirical
sections.summary: Three general design approaches are distinguished. Empirical design relies on experiments/experience to correlate inputs and outcomes (simple, real-world based, but valid only within the range of the underlying data). Mechanistic design uses mechanics theory (Westergaard's 1920s slab-on-subgrade for rigid; Burmister's 1940s multilayer elastic theory for flexible) to compute pavement responses, but a fully mechanistic design does not yet exist. Mechanistic-empirical (M-E) design combines both: mechanics computes responses (stresses, strains, deflections), which are then linked to performance through empirical distress models (e.g., AC-bottom tensile strain to fatigue cracking; subgrade compressive strain to rutting). The NCHRP 1-37A guide is the modern M-E procedure.
sections.body: The terms empirical, mechanistic, and mechanistic-empirical identify the general design approaches. EMPIRICAL design is based solely on experiments or experience: observations establish correlations between design inputs and performance outcomes; these relationships lack a firm scientific basis but must meet tests of engineering reasonableness (correct trends, correct limiting behavior). Their advantage is simplicity and grounding in real data; their disadvantage is that validity is limited to the conditions of the underlying data, so new materials, construction procedures, and traffic cannot be readily incorporated. MECHANISTIC design uses the theories of mechanics to relate pavement structural behavior and performance to traffic loading and environment. The rigid-pavement mechanistic approach originates with Westergaard's 1920s slab-on-subgrade and thermal-curling theories; the flexible approach with Burmister's 1940s multilayer elastic theory; both build on the Boussinesq/Burmister/Westergaard elasticity solutions. Because those solutions assume linear-elastic behavior, they cannot predict the nonlinear, inelastic cracking and permanent deformation of real pavements, which requires far more sophisticated material models. A fully mechanistic pavement design does not yet exist - some empirical relationships are still required to link theory to performance. MECHANISTIC-EMPIRICAL (M-E) design combines both: a mechanics-based determination of responses (stresses, strains, deflections) is related to performance through empirical distress models. For example, a linear-elastic model computes the tensile strain at the bottom of the AC layer, which is then related empirically to fatigue-cracking accumulation; early work used vertical compressive strain on top of the subgrade as a permanent-deformation (rutting) criterion (Kerkhoven and Dormon, 1953) and horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of the AC layer for fatigue (Saal and Pell, 1960). Several M-E procedures have been proposed (Asphalt Institute, PCA, AASHTO 1998 Supplement, NCHRP 1-26), culminating in the NCHRP 1-37A Pavement Design Guide.
key_points: Empirical design: correlations from experiments/experience; simple and data-based but valid only within the data range
Mechanistic design: mechanics theory (Westergaard rigid 1920s; Burmister flexible 1940s) computes responses; a fully mechanistic design does not yet exist
Mechanistic-empirical (M-E): mechanics computes responses, empirical distress models link them to performance
Classic M-E criteria: AC-bottom tensile strain -> fatigue cracking; subgrade-top compressive strain -> rutting
NCHRP 1-37A is the modern M-E design guide; 1993 AASHTO is the dominant empirical guide
sections.applicability: Choosing and understanding the design framework (empirical vs. M-E) into which geotechnical inputs feed
